sentences.text: On a summer night in 1899, in the mountains of Colorado, a man stood inside a wooden barn and waited for the sky to answer him.
He pressed a switch.
And a bolt of lightning, more than a hundred feet long, roared out of a metal ball on top of his tower.
The thunder was heard fifteen miles away.
Sparks jumped from the ground to the feet of horses.
And in the town nearby, the power station burst into flames.
The man in the barn was Nikola Tesla.
He was the inventor who lit the modern world.
He sent electricity through the air.
He controlled a boat with invisible waves.
He claimed he could split the Earth in two.
Some of his experiments changed history.
Some of them were never explained.
This is the story of the experiments of Nikola Tesla.
Chapter One.
The Boy and the Lightning.
Nikola Tesla was born at midnight, on the tenth of July, 1856, in a small village called Smiljan, in what is now Croatia.
According to family legend, he was born during a violent thunderstorm.
The midwife said it was a bad sign.
A child of the storm.
His mother disagreed.
"No," she said.
"He will be a child of light."
As a boy, Nikola had a strange gift.
He could see inventions in his mind so clearly that they seemed real.
He could build a machine in his head, run it for weeks, and then check which parts had worn down.
He never needed drawings.
The workshop was inside his own skull.
At the Polytechnic school in Graz, Austria, his professor showed the class a new electric machine.
It ran on direct current, and it sparked and crackled every time it turned.
Young Tesla stood up and said that one day, someone would build a motor without those sparks.
The professor laughed at him in front of the whole class.
He said it was like trying to build a perpetual motion machine.
Impossible.
Tesla never forgot that laugh.
Chapter Two.
A Vision in the Park.
In 1882, in Budapest, Tesla was walking through a city park at sunset with a friend, reciting poetry.
Suddenly, he stopped.
In his mind, he saw it.
A magnetic field that spun in a circle, like an invisible whirlpool, dragging a motor around with it.
No sparks.
No brushes.
No wasted energy.
He grabbed a stick and drew the diagram in the dirt.
It was the rotating magnetic field.
And it was the key to alternating current, the kind of electricity that flows through the walls of your home right now.
There was only one problem.
Nobody believed him.
Chapter Three.
Tesla Versus Edison.
In 1884, Tesla arrived in New York with almost nothing in his pockets, and a letter of introduction to the most famous inventor in the world.
Thomas Edison.
Edison hired him.
Tesla worked day and night, fixing Edison's machines and improving his generators.
Tesla later said Edison had promised him fifty thousand dollars if he could redesign the generators.
When he finished and asked for the money, Edison reportedly smiled and said, "Tesla, you don't understand our American humor."
Tesla quit.
For a time, the man who would light the world was so poor that he dug ditches in the streets of New York for two dollars a day.
But he did not give up.
In 1887, he finally found investors, opened his own laboratory, and built his alternating current motor.
It worked perfectly.
A businessman named George Westinghouse bought his patents.
And a war began.
They called it the War of the Currents.
Edison's direct current could only travel about a mile before it faded.
Tesla's alternating current could travel hundreds of miles.
Edison fought back with fear.
His allies held public demonstrations, killing animals with alternating current to prove it was deadly.
They even helped build the first electric chair, and made sure it ran on alternating current.
But Tesla had his own weapon.
Showmanship.
In 1893, at the World's Fair in Chicago, Westinghouse and Tesla lit up the entire fair with alternating current.
Nearly a hundred thousand lights blazed at once.
Twenty-seven million visitors saw the future with their own eyes.
Then came the ultimate test.
Niagara Falls.
In 1896, Tesla's system turned the power of the waterfall into electricity, and sent it twenty-six miles to the city of Buffalo.
The War of the Currents was over.
Alternating current had won.
And then Tesla did something no businessman would ever do.
Westinghouse's company was in deep financial trouble.
Tesla's contract would have paid him royalties on every unit of electricity sold.
It could have made him the richest man on Earth.
He tore up the contract.
He gave away a fortune to save the company that believed in him.
Chapter Four.
The Wizard of Light.
Now Tesla turned his mind to something even stranger.
Electricity at very high frequencies.
In 1891, he invented the Tesla coil.
A machine that could create millions of volts, and throw purple lightning across a room.
He began to give lectures that felt more like magic shows.
In front of crowds of scientists, he held glass tubes in his bare hands, and they lit up.
No wires.
No plugs.
Just light, glowing out of the air.
Then he did something that made the audience gasp.
He let hundreds of thousands of volts pass through his own body.
Sparks flew from his fingertips.
His body glowed with a strange purple halo.
And he smiled.
The current was so fast, it flowed over the surface of his skin instead of through his heart.
He was not harmed.
Newspapers called him a wizard.
But in March 1895, disaster struck.
A fire tore through his laboratory on Fifth Avenue in New York.
Years of notes, machines, and experiments were destroyed in a single night.
Tesla had no insurance.
He was devastated.
But within months, he was experimenting again.
In 1895, before almost anyone else in America, he was making images of bones through human flesh, using invisible rays.
Shadowgraphs, he called them.
We call them X-rays.
He took images of his own skull, and his own hand.
And he warned that the rays could burn the skin.
He was right.
Chapter Five.
The Invisible Hand.
In 1898, at Madison Square Garden in New York, Tesla unveiled his most mysterious invention yet.
A small boat sat in a pool of water.
Tesla stood at the side of the room, holding a box.
When the audience called out commands, the boat obeyed.
It turned left.
It turned right.
It flashed its lights.
There were no wires.
Nobody was inside.
The audience was stunned.
Some thought it was a trick.
Some thought a trained monkey was hidden inside.
One person suggested Tesla was controlling it with his mind.
In truth, he was controlling it with radio waves.
It was the world's first remote-controlled vehicle.
The ancestor of every drone, every remote, and every robot.
Tesla even predicted that one day, machines like this would fight wars without soldiers.
Around this time, a strange story began to spread across New York.
Tesla had built a small mechanical oscillator, a device that vibrated at a steady rhythm.
According to the legend, he attached it to an iron pillar in his laboratory, and slowly tuned the vibration.
The building began to shake.
Then the buildings around it.
Windows rattled.
Neighbors ran into the street.
Police raced to his lab.
Tesla supposedly smashed the machine with a hammer just in time.
Later, he claimed that with the right vibration, he could bring down any building, and even split the Earth itself.
Nobody knows how much of the story is true.
But it made Tesla a legend.
Chapter Six.
The Lightning Barn.
In 1899, Tesla moved to Colorado Springs, high in the Rocky Mountains, where the air was thin and lightning storms were common.
There, he built a giant laboratory with a tower nearly two hundred feet tall, topped with a copper ball.
Inside, he built his greatest machine.
The magnifying transmitter.
A Tesla coil so powerful that it could create artificial lightning.
On the night he turned it on at full power, the bolts were more than a hundred feet long.
The roar could be heard for miles.
And then, everything went dark.
Tesla had drawn so much power that he burned out the generator at the city's power station.
He had to pay to fix it himself.
In Colorado, Tesla was chasing one dream.
To send electricity through the Earth itself, so that power could be pulled from the ground anywhere in the world, without a single wire.
He claimed that he lit two hundred lamps placed miles away, without any wires at all.
And late one night, alone with his radio receiver, he heard something strange.
A rhythmic pattern of signals.
One.
Two.
Three.
Tesla became convinced he was hearing a message from another planet.
Possibly Mars.
Scientists laughed at him again.
Today, some believe he may have picked up natural radio waves from space.
Others think he heard signals from another radio experiment.
We will never know for sure.
Chapter Seven.
The Tower.
In 1901, Tesla began building the project of his life.
On Long Island, New York, he raised a massive tower, almost two hundred feet tall, with a giant dome on top.
It was called Wardenclyffe.
The tower was meant to send messages, pictures, and voices across the ocean.
And one day, to send free electricity to the entire world.
The richest banker in America, J.P. Morgan, gave him one hundred and fifty thousand dollars to build it.
But while Tesla was still building, an Italian inventor named Guglielmo Marconi sent the first radio signal across the Atlantic Ocean.
Tesla was furious.
He believed Marconi had used his patents.
"Marconi is a good fellow," Tesla said.
"Let him continue.
He is using seventeen of my patents."
Then Morgan asked a simple question.
If electricity was free, and anyone could pull it from the ground, where would he put the meter?
How would anyone make money?
Morgan stopped the funding.
Tesla begged.
He wrote letter after letter.
But the money never came back.
The tower stood unfinished for years.
In 1917, it was blown up with dynamite and sold for scrap.
His greatest dream was gone.
Chapter Eight.
The Last Experiments.
Tesla grew older, poorer, and more alone.
But he never stopped imagining.
He designed a turbine with no blades, using smooth spinning discs.
He drew plans for flying machines that could take off straight up, like helicopters.
At seventy-eight, he announced he had invented a "death beam" that could bring down ten thousand airplanes from two hundred miles away.
He called it a weapon to end all war.
Nobody ever saw it.
In his final years, Tesla lived alone in room 3327 of the Hotel New Yorker.
He spent his days feeding the pigeons in the park.
He said one white pigeon was the love of his life.
On the seventh of January, 1943, Nikola Tesla died in his hotel room.
He was eighty-six years old.
He owned almost nothing.
Within hours, government agents arrived and took away his papers.
Months later, the United States Supreme Court ruled on a long patent battle over the invention of radio.
Tesla's earlier patent was upheld.
He did not live to see it.
Epilogue.
Today, Tesla's alternating current powers almost every home on Earth.
His ideas live inside radios, remote controls, wireless chargers, and electric motors.
The scientific unit of magnetic power is named after him.
The tesla.
He held around three hundred patents.
He sent light through the air.
He made lightning in the mountains.
And he dreamed of a world where energy was free, for everyone.
The world laughed at him many times.
But in the end, Nikola Tesla did exactly what his mother said he would do.
He became a child of light.
